notes.front: What is a support entitlement?
notes.back: The right to create, view and comment on support tickets associated with an enterprise account.
notes.explanation: Without one, a member cannot open tickets on behalf of the enterprise account itself.
notes.example: Like a name on a company’s approved-callers list for a supplier’s help desk.
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners and billing managers automatically have a support entitlement, which enables them to create, view, and comment on support tickets associated with their enterprise account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “About support entitlement”

notes.front: What is GitHub Premium Support?
notes.back: A paid support plan GitHub Enterprise customers can add on top of Enterprise Support, including round-the-clock written support in English.
notes.explanation: It is sold in addition to all the benefits of GitHub Enterprise Support, not as a replacement for them.
notes.example: Like upgrading a car’s standard warranty to a premium plan with a guaranteed call-out time.
notes.evidence: In addition to all of the benefits of GitHub Enterprise Support, GitHub Enterprise customers can purchase GitHub Premium Support, which offers: * Written support, in English, through our support portal 24 hours per day, 7 days per week
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “About GitHub Support”

notes.front: What is a diagnostic file, for GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES)?
notes.back: A plain-text overview of an instance’s settings and environment that GitHub Support may request.
notes.explanation: It is one of the types of data Support may request to troubleshoot an instance in your environment.
notes.example: Like the printout a mechanic takes from a car’s computer before looking under the bonnet.
notes.evidence: To help you troubleshoot issues with a GitHub Enterprise Server instance in your environment, GitHub Support may request one or more types of data. | Data | File format | Description | | :---------------------- | :---------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Diagnostic file | Plaintext | Contains information about the instance's settings and environment. |
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “About diagnostic files and support bundles”

notes.front: What is a support bundle?
notes.back: An archive of a GHES instance’s diagnostics and sanitised log files, from the past two days by default.
notes.explanation: GitHub Support may ask for one after you submit a request, to see logs as well as settings.
notes.example: Like sending a mechanic both the car’s computer printout and its recent trip recordings.
notes.evidence: After you submit your support request, we may ask you to share a support bundle with our team. The support bundle is a gzip-compressed tar archive that includes diagnostics and important logs from your instance
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing support bundles”

notes.front: What is an extended support bundle?
notes.back: A support bundle holding logs from the past eight days rather than two.
notes.explanation: GitHub Support may ask for one when the events it is investigating happened more than two days ago.
notes.example: Like handing over a week of dashcam footage when the incident was last Tuesday.
notes.evidence: Support bundles include logs from the past two days by default, while *extended* support bundles include logs from the past eight days. If the events that GitHub Support is investigating occurred more than two days ago, we may ask you to share an extended support bundle.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing extended support bundles”

notes.front: What is a release on GitHub?
notes.back: A deployable software iteration, based on a Git tag, packaged with release notes and links to binary files for others to download.
notes.explanation: The tag marks a point in the repository’s history, and a tag’s date can differ from the release’s because they can be created at different times.
notes.example: Like a labelled edition of a book sent to shops, fixed to a particular draft of the manuscript.
notes.evidence: Releases are deployable software iterations you can package and make available for a wider audience to download and use. Releases are based on Git tags, which mark a specific point in your repository's history. A tag date may be different than a release date since they can be created at different times.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About releases”, “About releases”

notes.front: Who has a support entitlement automatically, and who can add more?
notes.back: Enterprise owners and billing managers have one; enterprise owners can add entitlements for members of the enterprise’s organisations.
notes.explanation: Members given an entitlement can then create, view and comment on the enterprise’s support tickets too.
notes.evidence: Enterprise owners can also add support entitlements to members of organizations owned by their enterprise account, allowing those members to create, view, and comment on support tickets.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “About support entitlement”

notes.front: A platform engineer, an ordinary organisation member, must open a ticket about an enterprise-wide SAML problem. They see no Enterprises section when choosing the account. What fixes this?
notes.back: A: an enterprise owner adds a support entitlement.
notes.choices:
A) An enterprise owner adds a support entitlement for the engineer
B) Ask any organisation member to open it instead
C) Make the engineer a billing manager of one organisation
D) Buy GitHub Premium Support
notes.choicesExplained: Organisation billing managers cannot be added in enterprise-owned organisations, and it would not give enterprise ticket rights. Other plain members lack the entitlement too. Premium Support changes the service level, not who may open tickets.
notes.explanation: Tickets on the enterprise account itself need an entitlement, which enterprise owners can grant to members.
notes.evidence: To open, view, and comment on support tickets associated with an enterprise account, you must have support entitlements for the enterprise. Enterprise owners and billing managers automatically have a support entitlement, and enterprise owners can add support entitlements to enterprise members.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating a support ticket”, “About support tickets”

notes.front: A developer with no support entitlement wants help with a problem in one organisation owned by the enterprise. What is true?
notes.back: A: any organisation member can create a ticket for that organisation.
notes.choices:
A) Any organisation member can create a ticket for that organisation
B) Only enterprise owners can open any ticket
C) They must first be granted a support entitlement
D) Organisation issues must go through GitHub Sales
notes.choicesExplained: Enterprise owners are not the only ones allowed. An entitlement is needed only for tickets on the enterprise account itself. Sales handles pricing and licensing, not support issues.
notes.explanation: The entitlement rule covers only tickets associated with the enterprise account.
notes.evidence: Any organization member can create tickets associated with an individual organization that is owned by an enterprise account. Support entitlements are only required to create tickets associated with the enterprise account itself.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating a support ticket”, “About support tickets”

notes.front: What are two things GitHub asks you to include in a support ticket?
notes.back: Two of: full URLs, repository names and usernames; exact wording of error messages; steps to reproduce; relevant logs and screenshots.
notes.explanation: GitHub Support has no access to private or internal resources, so complete details mean less back-and-forth.
notes.evidence: GitHub Support does not have access to any private or internal GitHub resources. Providing GitHub Support with everything they need to understand, locate, and reproduce an issue will allow for a faster resolution and less back-and-forth between yourself and the support team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating a support ticket”, “What to include in your support ticket”

notes.front: An administrator of an enterprise on GHE.com signs in to the GitHub Support portal with their GitHub.com account and opens a ticket about the data-resident enterprise. What happens?
notes.back: A: they will be asked to open a new ticket signed in with their GHE.com account.
notes.choices:
A) They will be asked to open a new ticket signed in with their GHE.com account
B) The ticket is closed as out of scope
C) Support converts the account for them
D) The ticket is routed automatically to the GHE.com team
notes.choicesExplained: No automatic routing is described. Data residency is in scope. Support does not convert accounts; the rule is to sign in with the GHE.com account.
notes.explanation: Tickets about a data-resident enterprise must come from the GHE.com account.
notes.evidence: If your enterprise uses data residency, you must sign in with your GHE.com account when creating a support ticket about your data-resident enterprise. Otherwise, you will be asked to open a new ticket using your GHE.com account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating a support ticket”, “Creating a support ticket”

notes.front: What are two kinds of request that are possibly outside GitHub Support’s scope?
notes.back: Two of: third-party integrations; configuring external authentication such as SAML identity providers; writing scripts; preview features; cloud network setup.
notes.explanation: The docs say “possibly”: these are signs a request may fall outside scope, not fixed exclusions.
notes.evidence: Your support request is possibly out of GitHub Support's scope if the request is primarily about: * Third party integrations, such as Jira * CI/CD, such as Jenkins * Azure DevOps (please contact Azure Support) * Writing scripts * Configuration of external authentication systems, such as SAML identity providers
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “Scope of support”

notes.front: Which request is most likely inside GitHub Support’s scope?
notes.back: D: an error with a generally available GitHub feature.
notes.choices:
A) Fixing claim mappings inside the company’s SAML identity provider
B) Writing a script to bulk-rename repositories
C) Tuning a Jenkins pipeline that pushes to GitHub
D) An error when enabling a generally available enterprise feature on GitHub
notes.choicesExplained: Configuring external authentication systems such as SAML identity providers is possibly out of scope. So are writing scripts and build tools such as Jenkins.
notes.explanation: The scope list names external systems, scripting and preview features; a GitHub feature misbehaving is none of those.
notes.evidence: Writing scripts * Configuration of external authentication systems, such as SAML identity providers * Open source projects * Writing or debugging new queries for CodeQL
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “Scope of support”

notes.front: An enterprise hits a bug in a feature that is in public preview. Where should it go for help?
notes.back: A: the account manager on GitHub’s Sales team.
notes.choices:
A) Its account manager on GitHub’s Sales team
B) A GitHub Support ticket, which covers previews fully
C) The GitHub Status page
D) GitHub Premium Support only
notes.choicesExplained: Public, private and technical previews are out of GitHub Support’s scope, with or without Premium Support. The Status page reports incidents; it does not take requests.
notes.explanation: Preview features sit outside Support’s scope, so the docs route public-preview help through the account manager.
notes.evidence: For support with public preview features, you can contact your account manager on GitHub's Sales team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “Scope of support”

notes.front: Will GitHub Support explain why an enterprise’s metered Actions spending rose last month?
notes.back: No. Support does not interpret usage reporting or spending trends for metered billing products.
notes.explanation: Nor will Support give recommendations based on that usage data.
notes.evidence: Metered billing explanations. GitHub Support does not interpret usage reporting or spending trends for metered GitHub billing products, nor provide recommendations based on that data.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “Scope of support”

notes.front: An instance runs a discontinued GHES release. What must happen before GitHub Support can help?
notes.back: Upgrade to a supported version, then open the ticket.
notes.explanation: GitHub Support does not provide support for discontinued GitHub Enterprise Server releases.
notes.evidence: GitHub Support does not provide support for discontinued GitHub Enterprise Server releases. If you're running a discontinued release, please upgrade to a supported version before opening a support ticket so we can help you effectively.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating a support ticket”, “Support for discontinued GitHub Enterprise Server releases”

notes.front: A team running an old GHES release that is no longer supported reports slow page loads and asks GitHub Support to investigate as it is. What will Support ask first?
notes.back: C: upgrade to a supported release first.
notes.choices:
A) A support bundle from the old release
B) An extended support bundle covering eight days
C) That they upgrade to a supported release before opening the ticket
D) That they buy GitHub Premium Support
notes.choicesExplained: Bundles from a discontinued release do not change the rule, however long they cover. Premium Support does not extend support to discontinued releases.
notes.explanation: Discontinued releases are outside support altogether, so the upgrade comes before the ticket.
notes.evidence: If you're running a discontinued release, please upgrade to a supported version before opening a support ticket so we can help you effectively.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Creating a support ticket”, “Support for discontinued GitHub Enterprise Server releases”

notes.front: What should you check before contacting GitHub Support?
notes.back: GitHub Status, for active incidents affecting GitHub services.
notes.explanation: GitHub Status lists the incidents currently affecting GitHub services.
notes.evidence: Before contacting GitHub Support, check GitHub Status for any active incidents affecting GitHub services.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “About GitHub Support”

notes.front: GitHub Support asks for temporary access to a private repository. How long does the owner have to reply, and how long does access last?
notes.back: Twenty days to accept or decline; if accepted, five days of access.
notes.explanation: If the owner does nothing, the request expires once the 20 days are up.
notes.evidence: The owner will have 20 days to accept or decline the request before the request expires. If the owner accepts the request, GitHub Support will have access to the repository for five days.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “Granting GitHub Support temporary access to a private repository”

notes.front: During temporary access, GitHub Support staff can unlock a private repository for up to {{c1::two hours}} at a time.
notes.explanation: Staff relock the repository early if the work is completed sooner.
notes.evidence: During this window, GitHub Support staff with the required privileges can unlock the repository for up to two hours at a time, and will relock the repository if the work is completed early.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Support”, “Granting GitHub Support temporary access to a private repository”

notes.front: What are two kinds of information a GHES diagnostic file contains?
notes.back: Two of: licence information; version numbers; network settings; authentication method; numbers of repositories and users.
notes.explanation: It is an overview of the instance’s settings and environment, not its logs.
notes.evidence: Diagnostic files are an overview of a GitHub Enterprise Server instance's settings and environment that contain: * Client license information, including company name, expiration date, and number of user licenses
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing diagnostic files”

notes.front: GitHub Support wants an overview of a GHES instance’s settings. The administrator has no command-line access to the instance but can sign in to the Management Console. What should they send?
notes.back: A: a diagnostic file from the Management Console.
notes.choices:
A) A diagnostic file downloaded from the Management Console
B) An extended support bundle
C) The enterprise audit log
D) A license report
notes.choicesExplained: An extended bundle needs command-line (`ssh`) access and holds logs rather than a settings overview. The audit log records events, not settings. A license report covers seats, not the instance’s environment.
notes.explanation: Diagnostics can be downloaded from the Management Console or with the `ghe-diagnostics` utility.
notes.evidence: You can download the diagnostics for your instance from the Management Console or by running the `ghe-diagnostics` command-line utility.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing diagnostic files”

notes.front: How many days of logs does a support bundle hold, and can you change it?
notes.back: Two days by default; you can specify an exact duration in days.
notes.explanation: For eight days of logs, the extended support bundle is the option the docs name.
notes.evidence: Support bundles include logs from the past two days by default. You can specify an exact duration in days. To provide logs from the past eight days, you can download an extended support bundle.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing support bundles”

notes.front: How do you create an extended support bundle, and can the Management Console do it?
notes.back: Over `ssh`, adding `-x` to `ghe-support-bundle`, e.g. `ghe-support-bundle -o -x`; the Management Console cannot.
notes.explanation: You need command-line access to the instance to download an extended bundle.
notes.evidence: You will need SSH access to download an extended bundle - you cannot download an extended bundle from the Management Console.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing extended support bundles”

notes.front: A GHES outage happened five days ago. GitHub Support needs logs covering it. What should the administrator provide?
notes.back: C: an extended support bundle.
notes.choices:
A) A diagnostic file
B) A support bundle with default settings
C) An extended support bundle
D) Screenshots of the monitor dashboards
notes.choicesExplained: A diagnostic file has settings, not logs. A default bundle covers only the past two days. Dashboard screenshots show metrics, not the logs Support asked for.
notes.explanation: Extended bundles hold eight days of logs, enough to reach an event five days back.
notes.evidence: | Support bundle | Archive | Contains a diagnostics file and sanitized log files from the past two days by default. | | Extended support bundle | Archive | Contains a diagnostics file and sanitized log files from the past eight days. |
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “About diagnostic files and support bundles”

notes.front: What is removed from the logs in a support bundle or diagnostics file?
notes.back: Authentication tokens, keys and secrets, in the listed log directories.
notes.explanation: The removal applies to logs in the directories the docs list, in both bundles and diagnostics files.
notes.evidence: Authentication tokens, keys, and secrets are removed from log files in the following log directories contained within a support bundle or diagnostics file:
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “About log file sanitization”

notes.front: Why might a support bundle lack some older logs?
notes.back: Bundles contain only logs that have not been rotated and compressed.
notes.explanation: This keeps bundles from becoming too large; rotation runs daily or weekly depending on the log file.
notes.evidence: To prevent bundles from becoming too large, bundles only contain logs that haven't been rotated and compressed. Log rotation on GitHub Enterprise Server happens at various frequencies (daily or weekly) for different log files
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Providing data to GitHub Support”, “Creating and sharing extended support bundles”

notes.front: Which GHES monitor dashboard is shown by default, and where are the dashboards?
notes.back: The “Operational Health” dashboard, under Monitor in the Management Console.
notes.explanation: It visualises key metrics for a quick look at the appliance’s health.
notes.evidence: This is the default dashboard displayed on the "Monitor" page. It visualizes key metrics that help you to get a quick overview of the health of your GitHub Enterprise Server appliance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About the monitor dashboards”, ““Operational Health” dashboard”

notes.front: You edit a pre-built GHES monitor dashboard but cannot save the change. What should you do?
notes.back: Make a copy of the dashboard and customise the copy.
notes.explanation: Pre-built dashboards can be opened and edited for inspection only; copies keep your changes.
notes.evidence: Pre-built dashboards can be opened and edited for inspection, but changes cannot be saved. Create a copy of a dashboard to apply and retain any customizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About the monitor dashboards”, “Creating new dashboards”

notes.front: In GitHub flow, why make a separate branch for each set of unrelated changes?
notes.back: It makes review easier, keeps changes easy to revert or build on, and stops a delay in one set holding up the others.
notes.explanation: Separate branches also help future collaborators understand each change.
notes.evidence: Make a separate branch for each set of unrelated changes. This makes it easier for reviewers to give feedback. It also makes it easier for you and future collaborators to understand the changes and to revert or build on them. Additionally, if there is a delay in one set of changes, your other changes aren't also delayed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Make changes”

notes.front: Why does GitHub flow say to delete a branch after its pull request is merged?
notes.back: It shows the work is complete and stops people accidentally using old branches.
notes.explanation: A merged branch left in place can be mistaken for live work and built on by accident, which is the confusion deleting it prevents.
notes.evidence: After you merge your pull request, delete your branch. This indicates that the work on the branch is complete and prevents you or others from accidentally using old branches. For more information, see Deleting and restoring branches in a pull request. Don't worry about losing information. Your pull request and commit history will not be deleted.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Delete your branch”

notes.front: A developer’s pull request has one approval, but GitHub will not let them merge into `main`. The repository follows GitHub flow. What is the most likely reason?
notes.back: C: branch protection needs more or specific approvals.
notes.choices:
A) The branch must be deleted before merging
B) GitHub flow forbids merging into the default branch
C) Branch protection requires more approvals or one from a specific team
D) Pull requests can only be merged by enterprise owners
notes.choicesExplained: GitHub flow ends with merging into the default branch. Deleting comes after merging. Anyone with write permission can merge.
notes.explanation: Branch protection settings may block a merge until the pull request meets set review requirements.
notes.evidence: Branch protection settings may block merging if your pull request does not meet certain requirements. For example, you need a certain number of approving reviews or an approving review from a specific team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “GitHub flow”, “Merge your pull request”

notes.front: What are two rules that many enterprises apply to important branches through rulesets?
notes.back: Two of: restrict deletions; require a pull request for all changes; require status checks and deployments to succeed before merging.
notes.explanation: Each rule has a stated purpose: no accidental deletion, a paper trail with enforced reviews, and a guard against errors in production.
notes.evidence: * **Restrict deletions**, so you can be confident users won't accidentally delete the branch * **Require a pull request** for all changes, so you have a paper trail and can enforce reviews * **Require status checks and deployments to succeed** before merging pull requests, so you can guard against errors in production
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Establishing a governance framework for your enterprise”, “Protecting your branches”

notes.front: Under “Require a pull request before merging”, must the pull request be approved?
notes.back: Not necessarily: it must be opened, but approval is a separate, optional setting.
notes.explanation: Opening the pull request is what the rule demands; approval is a separate requirement.
notes.evidence: You can require that all changes to the target branch be associated with a pull request. The pull request doesn't necessarily have to be approved, but it must be opened.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Available rules for rulesets”, “Require a pull request before merging”

notes.front: When reviews from code owners are required and a file has several owners, whose approval is needed?
notes.back: Any one of the code owners.
notes.explanation: The requirement is met by a single owner’s approval, not by all of them.
notes.evidence: If you do, any pull request that modifies content with a code owner must be approved by that code owner before the pull request can be merged into the protected branch. Note that if code has multiple owners, an approval from *any* of the code owners will be sufficient to meet this requirement.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Available rules for rulesets”, “Require a pull request before merging”

notes.front: What does dismissing stale pull request approvals do?
notes.back: An approval is dismissed when new commits change the diff, so the pull request needs approving again.
notes.explanation: GitHub records the diff at approval; if it changes, the old approval no longer covers what will be merged.
notes.evidence: Optionally, you can choose to dismiss stale pull request approvals when commits are pushed that affect the diff in the pull request. GitHub records the state of the diff at the point when a pull request is approved.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Available rules for rulesets”, “Require a pull request before merging”

notes.front: A security lead worries that someone could add unreviewed code to a pull request after it has been approved. Which review setting does the documentation call the safer choice for this?
notes.back: C: dismiss stale pull request approvals.
notes.choices:
A) Require approval from someone other than the last person to push
B) Require all comments to be resolved
C) Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed
D) Required reviewers for specific teams
notes.choicesExplained: Requiring another person’s approval of the last push is described as a compromise that keeps stale reviews. Resolving comments and team reviewers do not address changes made after approval.
notes.explanation: If you are concerned about pull requests being hijacked, the docs say it is safer to dismiss stale reviews.
notes.evidence: If you are concerned about pull requests being "hijacked" (where unapproved content is added to approved pull requests), it is safer to dismiss stale reviews.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Available rules for rulesets”, “Require a pull request before merging”

notes.front: With the “Required reviewers” rule, how many teams can you name, and how many approvals can each require?
notes.back: Up to 15 teams, each requiring 0 to 10 approvals.
notes.explanation: A team member’s approval counts only when the team has write permission or higher for the repository.
notes.evidence: You can specify up to 15 different teams, and for each team you can require a certain number of approvals from team members. For an approval from a team member to count, the team must have write permissions (or higher) for the repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Available rules for rulesets”, “Required reviewers”

notes.front: Which merge method adds all of a feature branch’s commits to the base branch together with a merge commit?
notes.back: The default “Merge pull request” option.
notes.explanation: It uses Git’s `--no-ff` option, so a merge commit is always created.
notes.evidence: When you click the default **Merge pull request** option on a pull request, all commits from the feature branch are added to the base branch in a merge commit. The pull request is merged using the `--no-ff` option.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About merge methods on GitHub”, “About merge methods on GitHub”

notes.front: Which merge method combines a pull request’s commits into a single commit?
notes.back: “Squash and merge”.
notes.explanation: The contributor’s individual commits from the topic branch are no longer seen on the default branch.
notes.evidence: When you select the **Squash and merge** option on a pull request, the pull request's commits are squashed into a single commit. Instead of seeing all of a contributor's individual commits from a topic branch, the commits are combined into one commit and merged into the default branch.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About merge methods on GitHub”, “Squashing your merge commits”

notes.front: Which merge method adds each commit to the base branch individually, without a merge commit?
notes.back: “Rebase and merge”.
notes.explanation: It keeps a linear history, but does so by rewriting the base branch’s history with new commits.
notes.evidence: all commits from the topic branch (or head branch) are added onto the base branch individually without a merge commit. In that way, the rebase and merge behavior resembles a fast-forward merge by maintaining a linear project history. However, rebasing achieves this by re-writing the commit history on the base branch with new commits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About merge methods on GitHub”, “Rebasing and merging your commits”

notes.front: A ruleset on `main` requires rebase merges, but the repository’s settings do not allow rebase merging. What happens to pull requests into `main`?
notes.back: D: merging is blocked.
notes.choices:
A) GitHub falls back to a squash merge
B) The ruleset wins and rebase is enabled automatically
C) The repository setting wins and a merge commit is made
D) Merging is blocked
notes.choicesExplained: There is no fallback method, and neither setting silently overrides the other.
notes.explanation: A merge method disabled in the repository and a different method required by the ruleset leave no allowed way to merge.
notes.evidence: Optionally, you can require a merge type of merge, squash, or rebase. This means the targeted branches may only be merged based on the allowed type. Additionally if the repository has disabled a merge method and the ruleset required a different method, the merge will be blocked.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Available rules for rulesets”, “Require a pull request before merging”

notes.front: A tester with read access to a repository wants to publish the next release. What can they do?
notes.back: C: view and compare releases, but not manage them.
notes.choices:
A) Publish it, since releases are public
B) Manage releases only through the API
C) View and compare releases, but not manage them
D) Nothing: read access hides releases
notes.choicesExplained: Publishing is managing, which needs write permission. The API follows the same permissions. Read access does let people see releases.
notes.explanation: Anyone with read access can view and compare releases; managing them needs write permission.
notes.evidence: Anyone with read access to a repository can view and compare releases, but only people with write permissions to a repository can manage releases.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About releases”, “About releases”

notes.front: A release fixes a security vulnerability. What should the maintainers also publish?
notes.back: A security advisory in the repository.
notes.explanation: GitHub reviews each published advisory and may use it to send Dependabot alerts to affected repositories.
notes.evidence: If a release fixes a security vulnerability, you should publish a security advisory in your repository. GitHub reviews each published security advisory and may use it to send Dependabot alerts to affected repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About releases”, “About releases”

notes.front: What limits apply to files attached to a release?
notes.back: Up to 1,000 assets per release, each under 2 GiB; no limit on total size or bandwidth.
notes.explanation: The caps apply to the number of files and the size of each file, not to the release as a whole.
notes.evidence: Up to 1000 release assets may be associated with a single release. Each file included in a release must be under 2 GiB. There is no limit on the total size of a release, nor bandwidth usage.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About releases”, “Storage and bandwidth quotas”

notes.front: How can release notes be produced?
notes.back: Written by hand, generated automatically from a default template, or from your own customised template.
notes.explanation: Templates, default or customised, let the notes be generated rather than typed.
notes.evidence: You can manually create release notes while managing a release. Alternatively, you can automatically generate release notes from a default template, or customize your own release notes template.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About releases”, “About releases”
